newsitem.title: CANADA: CanWest to explore options with Australia.
newsitem.headline: CanWest to explore options with Australia.

text.p: CanWest Global Communications Corp said on Friday it would explore mutually acceptable options to rectify what the Australian Broadcast Authority called a breach in foreign ownership rules in connection with CanWest's control of Australia's Ten television network.

CanWest said it was surprised by the ABA ruling, which concluded that CanWest breached the foreign ownership restrictions of the Broadcast Services Act (BSA) when it entered into financing arrangements to enable two unrelated Australian companies to purchase shares in Network Ten.
CanWest said it rejected the ABA's conclusions.

"We note that the ABA Report does not object to CanWest having increased its economic interest in Network Ten, but merely concludes that the transaction documents might, or could grant CanWest undue influence over the new shareholders. It is this 'potential' influence with which the ABA finds fault," CanWest Chief Executive Israel Asper said in a statement.
"CanWest rejects the validity of this conclusion," he said.
The ABA said CanWest must remedy the breach within six months.

Asper said CanWest intended to work with the ABA to explore "several mutually acceptable options" to rectify the breach and that before the ABA's ruling it tabled a plan whereby the shares in question would be sold to the public in a listed stock offering.

"However, the Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) has not yet ruled on the same transactions, so any dialogue between us will have to be conducted in accordance with the anticipated ruling by FIRB," Asper said.
He added that any restructuring would have to comply with Australia's long-term media ownership policy intentions.

"We don't want to resolve one issue only to find later that the solution doesn't work as a result of future government policy changes. For a resolution of this dispute to be fair, it must also cover future eventualities," Asper said.
CanWest said it had enjoyed an open and cooperative relationship with the ABA and intended to continue that conduct.

"We are comforted somewhat by the fact that the ABA has specifically concluded that there was no deliberate attempt by any of the parties to breach the rules, and that all parties intended that the transactions should comply with the rules and that therefore, any breach, if the ABA's view is upheld by the courts, was unintentional and inadvertent."
